source.title: The Optimal Ridge Penalty for Real-world High-dimensional Data Can Be Zero or Negative due to the Implicit Ridge Regularization
source.authors: Dmitry Kobak; Jonathan Lomond; Benoit Sanchez

record.tranche_reason: Tests risk as predictor dimensionality changes in linear regression, rather than testing the original claim in deep networks.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses deep-network double descent and cites related results, but those are not its own results. It reports relevant risk-versus-dimensionality results for a spiked-covariance linear model. The real-data ridge curves and the MNIST risk-versus-penalty results do not sweep model size or another claimed axis.
record.test_reason: In spiked-covariance linear regression (n=64), the study sweeps dimensionality p across the interpolation threshold. It reports risk for OLS and minimum-norm OLS, which peaks near p=n and then falls, and for optimal ridge, which has no peak. These are the study's own results on V4 and V6 in a non-deep model class. This is a new setting, not the original method.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that minimum-norm OLS generalizes well when n≪p and that positive ridge can give no improvement. They find the optimal ridge penalty can be negative, due to implicit regularization from low-variance predictors. They state their results do not explain deep neural networks. They present the p-sweep as in line with the parallel double-descent literature rather than as their main contribution.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses ridge and minimum-norm linear regression with predictor-dimensionality sweeps and random-feature augmentation, rather than deep-network size, training-time, or sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different optimal ridge behavior for spherical covariance (ρ = 0) and correlated predictors (ρ = 0.1); in the latter, the coefficient vector is aligned with the leading principal component. The negative optimal penalty also depends on dimensionality and sample size.

fits_no_version.finding: For p≳600 (n=64, ρ=0.1), and for MNIST random Fourier features (p=2000, n=64), the risk-minimizing ridge penalty is negative (λopt=−150 and ≈−80 respectively). The authors attribute this to implicit over-regularization from low-variance directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In heavily overparameterized linear regression with the signal aligned to high-variance directions, minimum-norm interpolation over-regularizes, so the optimal ridge penalty is zero or negative.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding q random predictors and fitting minimum-norm OLS is asymptotically equivalent to ridge regression (Theorem 1). With fixed variance 1, the number of added predictors acts as a regularization knob with an optimum qopt.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Excess random overparameterization with minimum-norm fitting acts as implicit ridge regularization.

record.problems: The relevant dimensionality-risk results use a specific spiked-covariance linear model, with the signal aligned to a high-variance direction. The text reports Nrep = 100 for the principal simulation but gives no uncertainty estimates for these risk curves. The study does not test deep networks, training epochs, or risk as sample size changes.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results on the claim’s stated size, epoch, or sample-size risk curves were reported. The real-data and MNIST examples sweep ridge penalty rather than model size; the MNIST example also reports negative-penalty risk behavior, not a claimed double-descent axis.

untested.parts: Sample size n is varied only to locate λopt (Figure 3), not to show test risk rising with n near the threshold.
Tested only for linear and minimum-norm regression with Gaussian spiked-covariance features. The classical U-shaped first descent is not shown. Other model classes are not tested.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Label-noise or variance as the driver of the peak (noise level σ² is fixed) and multiple peaks along a capacity axis are not tested.
No re-expression of risk against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Risk versus number of fixed-variance (var=1) random predictors q for p=50, n=64. The curve passes p+q=n and has a minimum at qopt; the text describes the minimum but not a peak height.

record.verdict_notes: The tranche is changed from T2 to T3: this is a new model class (linear regression) with its own results on V4 and V6. The study is not an original source. It predates the originals as a preprint (May 2018) and cites them. No uncertainty is reported on the risk curves. The real-data liver.toxicity and MNIST results sweep λ rather than capacity and are correctly left out. The MNIST multiple diverging peaks occur along negative λ, not along a capacity axis, so they do not bear on V6's multiple-descent part.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-size sweeps and the claimed peak near the size that just fits the training set.
Test risk as training sample size increases near the interpolation threshold. Sample size is varied only for the optimal ridge penalty.
The risk curve is tested in a spiked-covariance linear-regression setting, not across a broad range of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.

The study tests the effect of optimally tuned ridge regularization on the dimensionality-risk curve. It does not test whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether peaks split into multiple descents, or those mechanisms across settings.
No risk curve is re-expressed against an appropriate effective number of parameters.

rows.subject: spiked covariance model
rows.operation_detail: Varied predictor dimensionality p and measured expected normalized MSE for OLS below the interpolation threshold.
rows.value: With p = 10, OLS yielded near-optimal performance; as p increased, OLS began to overfit and each additional predictor increased MSE. Near p ≈ n = 64, expected MSE became very large.
rows.note: Reports the rising side and large risk near the interpolation threshold; the post-threshold behavior is recorded separately in R2.
rows.check: The state is fine. Only the rising branch and the peak at p≈n=64 are shown. There is no classical first descent: OLS is already near-optimal at p=10 and rises monotonically. The baseline is the oracle normalized MSE of about 0.09 (1/(α+1)), not 'not stated'.

source_check.correct: The best attainable normalized MSE is 1/(10+1) ≈ 0.09; OLS at p=10 is near this oracle baseline.
source_check.problem: The baseline is recorded as not stated, although the text gives the oracle normalized MSE.

rows.subject: spiked covariance model
rows.operation_detail: Varied predictor dimensionality p and measured expected normalized MSE for the minimum-norm OLS estimator above the interpolation threshold.
rows.baseline: Risk near p ≈ n = 64, described as very large
rows.value: As p increased further, the MSE of minimum-norm OLS quickly decreased again.
rows.note: The paper states that the plot uses p ∈ [10, 1000] and marks the dimensionalities corresponding to Figure 2a–d.
rows.check: None. This is the second descent of minimum-norm OLS for p>n, read against the large risk near p=n.

rows.subject: spiked covariance model
rows.operation_detail: Compared expected risk across dimensionalities using the optimal ridge estimator.
rows.baseline: Minimum-norm OLS risk; oracle risk is also shown as a reference
rows.value: The optimal ridge risk was close to oracle risk for all dimensionalities and did not show any divergence at p = n.
rows.note: The paper reports this as a comparison to the minimum-norm estimator and as the effect of optimally selected ridge regularization.
rows.check: Subject and condition are correct. Its baseline is the minimum-norm OLS curve (R1/R2). The text also notes that ridge's gain over minimum-norm OLS vanishes for p≫n.

rows.subject: spiked covariance model
rows.size_stated: p = 50 existing predictors; q up to 400 added predictors; n = 64
rows.operation_detail: Added random predictors and used minimum-norm OLS, measuring expected MSE as the total predictor count p + q changed.
rows.measure: Expected MSE versus number of random predictors q
rows.baseline: MSE at q = 0 is not stated
rows.value: As p + q approached n, MSE increased; after p + q became larger than n, minimum-norm shrinkage began and MSE decreased. q ≈ 200 was already close to the limiting performance.
rows.note: The text describes the increase toward n and decrease beyond n; this is a random-feature augmentation setting, not a neural-network sweep.
rows.check: The capacity axis is confounded: the added predictors' variance is λopt/q, so their scale shrinks as q grows. It is not a pure capacity sweep. Replicates are not stated; the reader marked them 'not stated' and they likely match Nrep=100. The baseline at q=0 is OLS at p=50 (Figure 4a square).

relationships.condition: Spiked-covariance linear regression, minimum-norm OLS, n=64, p∈[10,1000], and random-predictor augmentation with p=50
relationships.reason: Risk becomes very large near p≈n, then quickly decreases for p>n (R1, R2). The same rise to p+q=n and later fall appears with random predictors (R4).
relationships.display_finding: Risk became very large near p=n and quickly decreased for p>n, with random-predictor augmentation producing the same rise at p+q=n and subsequent fall.
